Division of San Francisco Bay Toll Crossings, “Report to Department of Public Works on the Southern Crossing of San Francisco Bay,” California Department of Public Works, 1955.

Source: [Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/southern-crossing-1955-12/mode/thumb)

The San Francisco Bay Bridge opened in 1936 and within one year it was handling 20 percent more traffic than the California Department of Public Works (CDPW) had projected; by the end of World War II the figure was 91 percent (CDPW, 13). In response the Joint Army-Navy Board (JANB) began discussing a southern crossing in 1946. The JANB would eventually endorse the idea, and in 1953, a state Assemblyman from San Mateo County named Richard Dolwig introduced legislation to move forward with the project (Adler, 33). In 1955, the CDPW proposed the crossing presented here. Even though the plan enjoyed support from the state government, JANB, San Francisco city government, and the governments of East Bay cities, [the southern crossing would be short-circuited by the Navy](https://www.imaginedsanfrancisco.org/description/1021#), which announced that it had a secret plan to test seaplanes and would not approve the bridge. Many versions of a Southern Crossing have been proposed since 1946, but the version shown here came closest to being realized.
